source_document.body:
The Pacific Maritime Association and International Longshore and Warehouse Union Local 26 reached a tentative contract agreement early Saturday, easing the threat of a strike at six terminals at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. The deal covers roughly 250 unarmed security workers known as watchmen and still needs approval from Local 26 members. The current contract will stay in effect until the ratification vote.
What’s Related
“We thank the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service and U.S. Department of Labor for their help, and the Local 26 bargaining committee for its work at the table,” the PMA said in a social media post. “This agreement provides certainty for the ports, for the cargo owners and workers throughout the supply chain who depend on them, and for the Southern California, regional and national economies .”
The danger of a strike
The watchmen make up about 2% of the ILWU workforce at Los Angeles and Long Beach, according to the PMA. But the six terminals where they work handle more than half of the two ports’ combined cargo, including roughly 85% of Long Beach’s volume and 33% of Los Angeles’ volume, the employer group estimates.
Dockworkers and marine clerks are covered by separate contracts. The PMA said it expected those workers to honor Local 26 picket lines, which could have halted ship loading and unloading and cut off truck access at affected terminals. The coastwide agreement covering about 22,000 longshore workers at 29 West Coast ports runs through 2028.
RELATED: Top 30 U.S. Ports Ranked By Container Imports In 2025
Even a short stoppage could have added to existing delays. Jabari Watt, senior director of operations at freight forwarder Flexport, said Los Angeles and Long Beach accounted for 37% of U.S. imports in October. Before the deal, he pointed to a rail backlog at Los Angeles and said delays could continue after terminals reopened.
“As of November 18, nearly half the imports waiting on on-dock rail at Los Angeles had been there nine days or more,” Watt said. “In 2012, a clerks’ strike idled 10 of the 14 container terminals for eight days. However long a stoppage lasts, those containers will still be in line when the gates reopen, so the delays would outlast the strike itself.”
What led to the tentative deal
The watchmen’s previous agreement expired in July 2025, and members continued working under extensions. Local 26 members authorized a strike, and the deadline moved several times in November. The two sides agreed to another short extension on Nov. 18, giving negotiators more time before the Saturday deadline.
Before the deal, the PMA said its offer included a $3,200 one-time bonus per member and would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The proposal also called for keeping fully employer-paid health care for active workers and retirees and raising annual pension benefits to as much as $93,200 for the longest-serving workers.
Visit Logistics Management to read Jeff Berman’s full story.
